parts: Design is a plan or drawing showing the appearance of something before it is made; in embroidery it is a decorative pattern that adds beauty to an article. Choose a design suited to age, sex, occasion and need (a bright red heavily decorated saree is wrong for a summer wedding with a baby). Five types: geometrical (lines, circles, squares, rectangles, triangles; e.g. a hut), simplified (slight curves and few details), naturalized (close to nature: flowers, leaves, birds), stylised (more curves and details, away from the natural form, more decorative and complicated) and abstract (no specific inspiration; uses only the texture, veins, pattern or colour of an object). A leaf can be shown as naturalized, simplified, stylised and abstract.
A design starts with a motif; when a motif is repeated at certain intervals over a surface it is called a pattern; repetition of the pattern creates a design.

A design may have to be enlarged or reduced to suit the article (a big flower on a diwan cover, a small one on a cushion cover). Steps: find the design, trace it on tracing paper, transfer the tracing with carbon paper to graph paper, then use the squares as a guide to draw it on larger squares (enlargement) or smaller squares (reduction); each part increases by the same amount in width and height so proportion is kept.
Selecting a design and planning the article

Factors: purpose (cartoons on children's wear), shape and size of the article, colour and texture of the fabric (light embroidery on delicate chiffon, heavy on thick cotton), occasion, sex and age of the wearer, effective use of the fabric background, decorating points of emphasis (collar, pocket, neckline) and comfort (not heavy or abrasive to the skin). Plan the article by asking who will use it, what for, where, when and how; e.g. an eco-friendly shopping bag needs light, strong, water-resistant, colour-fast, non-snagging fabric (canvas, jute, cotton), strong handles, bright colours suited to all ages and embroidery in proportion to the bag.

Six methods: (1) direct (free-hand pencil on thin or transparent fabrics such as lawn, organdie, georgette, with the fabric tight in a hoop); (2) carbon paper (carbon side down between fabric and design, trace with a dry ball pen; use white or yellow carbon on dark fabric and blue on light or white); (3) back tracing (draw on tracing paper, go over the back of the lines with 2B or 4B pencil, tape with the pencilled side to the fabric and trace; simplest, no costly equipment; for symmetrical designs draw a quarter and fold); (4) butter paper or perforated pattern (trace on butter paper, prick holes along the lines with a needle or an empty sewing machine, pin on the fabric, rub with a ball of cotton dipped in a paste of powdered blue and kerosene oil, blow off the excess); (5) glass plate and light (glass over chair arms with a bulb below; design on thin paper under the fabric, outline with a hard pencil); (6) template (a shape cut from card paper, for simple designs repeated many times; draw the outline and remove).
Divide the measured garment into equal squares with tailor's chalk and place motifs: horizontal, vertical, half drop, diagonal or border placement.
